### C-R6-01 — Joash–Jotham not “like David”; next “like David” is Hezekiah
**Claim:** Provan notes a curious authorial doubt about Davidic wholeheartedness from Joash through Jotham: Amaziah “did right” but was “not like David” (like Joash); no Judean king is again “like David” until Hezekiah (2 Kgs 18:3).
**Quote:** “Yet we shall not read of another Judean king who is ‘like David’ until we read of Hezekiah (2 Kgs. 18:3; contrast 15:3, 34). There seems to be some doubt in the authors’ minds about the wholeheartedness of the Davidic kings’ commitment to the LORD throughout the period from Joash to Jotham, but they have not revealed to us their reasons for holding this opinion.”
**Locus:** §47 on 14:1–6 (slice ¶ near 14:1–6)
**Targets:** [[hezekiah]], [[david]], [[kingship-in-israel]], [[1-2-kings]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]]

### C-R6-02 — Amaziah’s Jerusalem capture foreshadows later exile (Jehoiachin pattern)
**Claim:** Provan reads Amaziah’s defeat, temple/palace plunder, hostages, and “lived” (not “reigned”) after Jehoash as foreshadowing the later deportation of Judean kings—especially Jehoiachin still called “king” while Babylon rules.
**Quote:** “This first account in Kings of foreign capture of Jerusalem is very reminiscent of the second from last (2 Kgs. 24:8ff.) where we also read of a king (Jehoiachin) taken captive with hostages and of temple and palace being plundered. That king, of course, went on living (Hb. ḥyh, as in 2 Kgs. 14:17) in Babylon for many years afterwards, still called ‘king’ by the authors of Kings even though it was the king of Babylon who effectively ruled over Judah (2 Kgs. 25:27–30…).”
**Locus:** §47 on 14:15–22
**Targets:** [[jehoiachin]] NEW, [[1-2-kings]], [[kingship-in-israel]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]]

### C-R6-03 — Jehoash as real “king” over humbled Judah; chronology as power
**Claim:** Provan argues Jehoash’s “misplaced” concluding formulas and Azariah’s Elath rebuild “after the king rested with his fathers” present Jehoash as real power over Judah—chronology as political power, foreshadowing foreign regnal dating at the end of Kings.
**Quote:** “Chronology is an aspect of political power. Are the events of 2 Kings 14:13–20 being presented, then, as a foreshadowing of those of the closing chapters of the book?”
**Locus:** §47 on 14:15–22
**Targets:** [[1-2-kings]], [[kingship-in-israel]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]]

### C-R6-04 — Jeroboam II as second “Solomon” by grace, not piety
**Claim:** Jeroboam II restores Solomonic northern borders (Lebo Hamath to Sea of Arabah; Damascus and Hamath) not because he is good but because post-Elisha deliverance, Jehu promise, and divine compassion still operate; the son of this second Solomon will fall more spectacularly than Solomon’s.
**Quote:** “This is not because he is a good king (v. 24). It is, rather, because in this period immediately after Elisha’s death there is still deliverance to be found, in spite of idolatry. The promise to Jehu stands (2 Kgs. 10:30); the compassion of God is still active (13:23).” / “Judah ‘falls’ (v. 10), in fact, under Israelite dominion, and it is Jeroboam II of Israel, rather than Amaziah of Judah, who ends up as the Solomon figure of the chapter…”
**Locus:** §47 on 14:23–29 (and end of 14:7–14 discussion)
**Targets:** [[solomon]], [[elisha]], [[1-2-kings]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]]

### C-R6-05 — “LORD had not said” blot out Israel: exile not final end
**Claim:** Provan reads 14:27 against Deuteronomy and earlier Kings: God had not declared utter blotting out of Israel’s name; exile is coming (1 Kgs 14:15–16) but is not the end; covenant promises still force (13:23).
**Quote:** “To blot out the name of Israel from under heaven would be to destroy it utterly (Deut. 9:14), making forgiveness and restoration impossible (Deut. 29:20). This is something that the LORD had not said he would do… Israel will go into exile for its sins (1 Kgs. 14:15–16), but this will not be the end of Israel (1 Kgs. 8:33–51). God’s covenant promises are still in force (2 Kgs. 13:23).”
**Locus:** §47 Additional Notes on 14:27
**Targets:** [[1-2-kings]], [[deuteronomistic-history]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]]

### C-R6-06 — Fourth generation of Jehu ends; accumulated wrath bursts
**Claim:** With Jeroboam II’s death, Jehu’s fourth-generation promise is exhausted; Zechariah is assassinated and the dynasty removed the moment the “blockage” ends—impression of accumulated wrath.
**Quote:** “With the death of Jeroboam II, we have reached the ‘fourth generation’ of the divine promise to Jehu (2 Kgs. 10:30). We expect a return to the unstable government… That is what we now find.” / “We have the impression of accumulated wrath, ready to burst in upon Jehu the moment the blockage to the normal flow of events is removed.”
**Locus:** §48 intro and 15:8–12
**Targets:** [[1-2-kings]], [[kingship-in-israel]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]]

### C-R6-07 — Assyria replaces Aram; Menahem’s “comfort” temporary
**Claim:** Pul/Tiglath-Pileser’s arrival ends Jeroboam’s empire; Menahem buys friendship with silver—an ominous rehearsal of the Assyria that will exile Israel; Elisha (“God saves”) gives way to Menahem (“comforter”) and temporary comfort by money.
**Quote:** “Aram has given way to Assyria as the great northern enemy, and the deliverance of the past, represented by Elisha (‘God saves’), has given way to the very temporary comfort of the present, represented by Menahem (meaning ‘comforter’) and his money.”
**Locus:** §48 on 15:17–22
**Targets:** [[elisha]], [[1-2-kings]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]]

### C-R6-08 — Ahaz as particularly wicked; Davidic promise oddly uncited
**Claim:** Ahaz walks in ways of Israel’s kings, promotes fertility cult at high places, and practices child sacrifice (Molech); Provan finds the absence of the David promise disconcerting—last such absence with wicked Ahaziah nearly extinguished the house.
**Quote:** “It is surprising, then, that there is such a notable absence here of any reference to the promise to David (cf., by contrast, 1 Kgs. 15:4 and 2 Kgs. 8:19)…. Is the Davidic promise no longer in force? Is Judah is to be ‘driven out’ of the land for its sins?”
**Locus:** §49 on 16:1–4
**Targets:** [[davidic-covenant]], [[david]], [[1-2-kings]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]]

### C-R6-09 — Ahaz vassal to Assyria; religious innovations aesthetic, not forced
**Claim:** Ahaz buys Assyrian help against the Syro-Ephraimite threat and redesigns Solomonic temple fixtures (new altar, stands, Sea’s base); Provan rejects reading most changes as vassal requirements—primarily aesthetics and foreign influence, not foreign control.
**Quote:** “Yet there is no suggestion in the text that any of the changes were specifically required of him as a vassal. The implication of verse 10 (he saw … and sent) is that, at least in the case of the altar, it was simply a matter of aesthetics… Ahaz is presented as a king who is open to foreign influence in his religious policy… He is not presented as one who is under foreign control.”
**Locus:** §49 on 16:5–9 and 16:10–20
**Targets:** [[solomon]], [[1-2-kings]], [[kingship-in-israel]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]]

### C-R6-10 — 2 Kgs 17: delayed uprooting ends; Hoshea’s name cannot save
**Claim:** Long-delayed “uprooting/scattering” of Israel (1 Kgs 14:15) ends when deliverances (Elisha, Jeroboam, unnamed saviors) cease; Hoshea means “salvation” but, unlike the prophet, cannot fulfill the name; third siege of Samaria is last.
**Quote:** “The ‘uprooting’ and ‘scattering’ of Israel (1 Kgs. 14:15) has long been delayed because of God’s promises and character (2 Kgs. 10:30; 13; 14:23–29)…. And though his name promises much (Hoshea, ‘salvation’), he—unlike the prophet—will have no power to fulfill its promise.”
**Locus:** §50 intro
**Targets:** [[elisha]], [[1-2-kings]], [[deuteronomistic-history]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]]

### C-R6-11 — Hoshea “not as bad” but reform (if any) too late
**Claim:** Hoshea did evil “but not as the kings of Israel who were before him”; Provan surmises possible less-than-wholehearted Jeroboam cult / beginnings of reform—if so, too late; political play between Assyria and Egypt triggers Shalmaneser, imprisonment, capture, deportation.
**Quote:** “Is there some hint at a lack of wholeheartedness in his pursuit of Jeroboam’s sins (significantly not mentioned here), a hint at the beginnings, perhaps, of religious reform? If so, it was too late.”
**Locus:** §50 on 17:1–6
**Targets:** [[1-2-kings]], [[kingship-in-israel]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]]

### C-R6-12 — 2 Kgs 17:7–17: primary theological indictment (Exodus prologue + first commandment)
**Claim:** Authors explain northern end only by underlying sin against the LORD who brought Israel from Egypt—echoing Decalogue prologue; central failure is “no other gods,” with high places, fertility cult, idols, calves, Asherah, Baal, stiff-necked imitation of nations.
**Quote:** “The authors of Kings are interested only in the explanation that underlies all others: the Israelites had sinned against the LORD their God, who had brought them out of Egypt. The line echoes the prolog to the Ten Commandments in Exodus 20:2 and Deuteronomy 5:6… The basic requirement is that they must have ‘no other gods before him’ (Exod. 20:3; Deut. 5:7). It is this most central commandment that Israel forgot…”
**Locus:** §50 on 17:7–17
**Targets:** [[1-2-kings]], [[deuteronomistic-history]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]]

### C-R6-13 — Idolaters become like their idols; driven out like the nations
**Claim:** Provan stresses idolatry’s moral formation (became “worthless,” v. 15) and measure-for-measure fate: imitating nations the LORD drove out, Israel is now driven out of the land.
**Quote:** “They worshiped idols… and were fashioned in their image (became worthless, v. 15)…. In doing as they did, Israel has now met the same fate. The Israelites have been driven out of the promised land.”
**Locus:** §50 on 17:7–17
**Targets:** [[1-2-kings]], [[deuteronomistic-history]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]]

### C-R6-14 — Indictment catalog deliberately includes Judah’s sins (links to 1 Kgs 14; Ahaz)
**Claim:** Several sins in 17:7–17 (high places + stones + Asherah; “every high hill / spreading tree”; fire-sacrifice; divination) hitherto attach to Judah (esp. 1 Kgs 14:23; Ahaz 16:4, 15)—so the catalog implicates both kingdoms.
**Quote:** “Several of the references appear to be to religion, not in the northern kingdom, but in Judah. The combination high places … sacred stones and Asherah poles (vv. 9–10) has appeared thus far only in 1 Kings 14:23… An almost identical phrase appears in relation to Ahaz (2 Kgs. 16:4), and it is only in that passage that we have hitherto read of fire-sacrifice (v. 17).”
**Locus:** §50 on 17:7–17
**Targets:** [[1-2-kings]], [[deuteronomistic-history]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]]

### C-R6-15 — Both kingdoms warned; Davidic promise will not forever protect Judah
**Claim:** From early divided monarchy hints, through Ahaz, to 17:7–17: both kingdoms sinned and received prophetic warnings; without response Judah will share Israel’s fate; Davidic promise will not protect forever (cf. 1 Kgs 9:1–9).
**Quote:** “Both kingdoms have sinned, and both have received prophetic warnings (v. 13). The implication is that, in the absence of any response, Judah will indeed go the same way as Israel. The Davidic promise will not in the end protect it (cf. the threat of 1 Kgs. 9:1–9).”
**Locus:** §50 on 17:7–17
**Targets:** [[davidic-covenant]], [[1-2-kings]], [[deuteronomistic-history]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]]

### C-R6-16 — Jeroboam’s “great sin” and swr wordplay; ambiguous “all Israel” / mʾs
**Claim:** 17:18–23 specifies Jeroboam’s great sin as heart of northern apostasy (swr: they did not turn from cult → LORD removed them); Judah followed Israel’s practices; “all the people of Israel” (v. 20) and mʾs reject/reject may reach forward to embrace Judah.
**Quote:** “They failed to turn away (Hb. swr) from the cult he introduced… and so the LORD eventually removed them (Hb. swr) to Assyria (vv. 22–23). The way that Judah … followed the practices Israel had introduced is, however, highlighted (vv. 18–19)…. Does [all the people of Israel] refer only to the ‘Israel’ of verses 18 and 21…? Or does it reach forward in the story to embrace Judah—‘rejecting’ God’s decrees (Hb. mʾs, v. 15) and in the end being rejected by him (Hb. mʾs, v. 20)?”
**Locus:** §50 on 17:18–23
**Targets:** [[1-2-kings]], [[deuteronomistic-history]], [[davidic-covenant]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]]

### C-R6-17 — 17:25–33 ironic: mixed “worship” is not true worship of the one LORD
**Claim:** Provan resolves 17:33 vs 17:34 contradiction by irony: vv. 25–33 set up a local-god, polytheistic viewpoint the authors demolish; true worship is exclusive (Do not worship any other gods); exile produces no religious improvement.
**Quote:** “We must reckon, then, with the presence of irony in 2 Kings 17:25–33. It is not a passage meant to be taken at face value…. An intrinsic feature of true worship, they tell us, is its exclusivity. Mixed worship is not true worship of the God who has from the beginning demanded Do not worship any other gods (vv. 35, 37–38). What is clear by the end of the chapter, then, is that the exile of Israel has not led to any improvement in the religion of the people who dwell in the land.”
**Locus:** §50 on 17:24–41
**Targets:** [[1-2-kings]], [[deuteronomistic-history]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]]

### C-R6-18 — Starry hosts and sorcery in 17 anticipate Manasseh
**Claim:** “All the starry hosts” and sorcery (17:16–17) have not yet appeared in the narrative and recur only with Manasseh (21:3–6); the indictment embraces Judah’s past and future sins.
**Quote:** “It is interesting that neither this sin, nor that of sorcery (v. 17), has been introduced to us so far in the narrative. These sins will not be mentioned again until the account of Manasseh’s reign in 2 Kgs. 21 (cf. 21:3–6). The passage embraces not only the sins of Judah in the preceding narrative, then, but also those yet to come.”
**Locus:** §50 Additional Notes on 17:16
**Targets:** [[manasseh]] NEW, [[1-2-kings]], [[provan-1-2-kings-nibc]]

### C-R6-19 — Hezekiah as second David: removes high places at last
**Claim:** After kings “not quite like David” and Ahaz utterly unlike him, Hezekiah is the long-awaited second David who reforms worship—first to reverse the recurrent “high places were not removed” into “he removed the high places,” plus stones, Asherah, and Nehushtan.
**Quote:** “This is the king for whom we have been waiting, the second David who reforms Judean worship and makes it what it should be.” / “Hezekiah now appears as the one who at last addresses this issue: he removed the high places (Hb. hûʾ hēsîr ʾeṯ-habbāmôṯ, 2 Kgs. 18:4).”
**Locus:** §51 intro and 18:1–4

### C-R6-20 — Unique trust; LORD with him; anti-Ahaz rebellion against Assyria
**Claim:** In trust (ḇṭḥ) none among Judah’s kings was like Hezekiah; he held fast (ḏḇq) to God vs Solomon’s ḏḇq to foreign wives; only David and Hezekiah get “LORD was with him,” wartime success (śḵl), Philistine defeat; he refuses ʿḇḏ service to Assyria that Ahaz accepted.
**Quote:** “In at least one respect, the way in which he trusted in the LORD (v. 5), there was no one like him among all the kings of Judah…. Only of David and Hezekiah among the Davidic kings is it said that the LORD was with him (v. 7….) and that the king was successful in war…. As similar to David as he was, he was by the same token utterly dissimilar to Ahaz, for he would not continue to serve the king of Assyria… but rebelled against him.”

**Claim:** 18:9–12 retells Samaria’s fall to frame Hezekiah’s policy; contrast Moses-obedience of Hezekiah’s people vs north suggests different fate—but judgment fell under the north’s best king (17:2), so reforms may be too late.
**Quote:** “Yet we cannot forget that it was under the best of the northern kings that judgment fell (2 Kgs. 17:2). Is it possible that Hezekiah’s reforms have come too late to make any difference? Are we now to read of the end of Judah?”

### C-R6-22 — Sennacherib assault: Hezekiah’s tribute as regrettable lapse
**Claim:** Opening of the siege (18:13–16)—fortified cities fall; Hezekiah pays with temple/palace gold and confesses sin to a foreign king—is a disappointing prolog to his finest hour, not what 18:1–8 led readers to expect.
**Quote:** “For all that Hezekiah has been lauded as a king quite unlike anyone who preceded him, his first reaction to foreign attack is a familiar one; he raids the royal treasuries and the temple… We are presumably to regard it as a regrettable lapse—a disappointing prolog to what will turn out to be Hezekiah’s finest hour.”
**Locus:** §52 on 18:13–16

### C-R6-23 — Trust (ḇṭḥ) is the rhetorical battlefield; Rabshakeh’s double attack
**Claim:** Field commander’s speech centers trust (ḇṭḥ): Egypt is a splintered reed; Hezekiah’s removal of high places supposedly offends the LORD; Assyria may be LORD’s instrument (as in 17)—sowing doubt between unseen LORD and visible army.
**Quote:** “The issue at the heart of the field commander’s speech is precisely that of ‘trust’ (Hb. ḇṭḥ in v. 5 and in vv. 19, 20, 21, 22, 24…).” / “Is it not much more likely that he has sent the Assyrians to destroy Jerusalem (v. 25)?… Are the Judeans wise… to trust in the unseen LORD, when the all too visible Assyrian army stands at the gates…?”

### C-R6-24 — Blasphemy overreach: LORD as one powerless god vs true living God
**Claim:** Offering Assyria as alternative provider of life/land and ranking the LORD among powerless gods overreaches; like Arameans in 1 Kgs 20, Assyria misconceives divine reality—so siege outcome is theologically predictable.
**Quote:** “It is one thing to claim that the LORD will not deliver Jerusalem because Assyria is the LORD’s instrument of judgment (v. 25). It is quite another thing to claim that the LORD is simply one of many powerless gods and cannot deliver Jerusalem (vv. 33–35), and to offer oneself in the LORD’s place as the true provider of material blessings and life itself (vv. 31–32).”

### C-R6-33 — Manasseh: irrevocable judgment—dish, Samaria plumb, Ahab fate for David’s house

### Key theses (Provan, this slice)
1. **2 Kgs 17** is the theological hinge: Decalogue-rooted exclusive worship failed; catalog implicates Judah; Davidic promise will not forever shield the south; northern resettlement “worship” is ironic non-worship.
2. **Hezekiah** is the second David of unique trust; Sennacherib crisis is a ḇṭḥ contest; deliverance is for YHWH’s name and **David**—even the best king now lives by **grace**, not guaranteed piety.
3. **Manasseh** is the worst king; patience breaks into irrevocable, Ahab-like, dish-wiped judgment on city and (apparently) Davidic house.
4. **Josiah** is second Moses / best king / come **too late**; Huldah grants only personal delay; reforms change nothing of settled fate; death like Ahaziah ends the delay.
5. **Ending:** Solomonic glory dismantled; reverse exodus; **Jehoiachin at the table** is not mere cynicism but Joash-like hope that **grace may triumph over law** and 2 Sam 7 still hold.
6. **§57 Excursus:** Hezekiah/Josiah as messianic models across Jeremiah, Zechariah, Chronicles, Isaiah, and NT (temple cleansing, law-keeping, suffering, restoration, Armageddon victory); typology plus discipleship (trust, reform, costly obedience).
